claim: The slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship decreases during darkness.
source: We found a large change in the slope and a smaller change in the y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship during the dark condition (t-statistic of interaction effect (slope): 18.045, df = 806, p=2×10−61; t-statistic of change in y-intercept: −3.676, df = 806, p=0.0003; n = 15 mice) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (t-test) showing significant change in slope during dark condition, and visual evidence in Figure 1B showing the relationship between theta frequency and running speed in light vs dark conditions.

claim: The theta amplitude vs. running speed relationship does not change significantly during darkness.
source: In contrast, the theta amplitude vs. running speed relationship did not change significantly (t-statistic of interaction effect (slope): 1.7343, df = 806, p=0.0832; t-statistic of change in y-intercept: −1.764, p=0.0781; n = 15 mice) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing non-significant changes in theta amplitude vs running speed relationship, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Average running speed during light (11.6 ± 0.5 cm/s) slightly decreased during darkness by 0.89 ± 0.31 cm/s (7.7%) to 10.72 ± 1.4 cm/s.
source: The average running speed during light, 11.6 ± 0.5 cm/s, slightly decreased during darkness by 0.89 ± 0.31 cm/s (7.7%) to 10.72 ± 1.4 cm/s (mean ± s.e.m., p=0.0117, n = 15 mice, Wilcoxon's signed-rank test) (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of running speed with statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon's signed-rank test) and visual representation in Figure 1D.

claim: Running acceleration decreased from 20.8 ± 1.9 cm/s2 in the light condition by 1.7 ± 0.7 cm/s2 (8.0%) to 19.1 ± 2.3 cm/s2 in the dark condition.
source: Similarly, running acceleration also slightly decreased from 20.8 ± 1.9 cm/s2 in the light condition by 1.7 ± 0.7 cm/s2 (8.0%) to 19.1 ± 2.3 cm/s2 in the dark condition (p=0.0070, n = 15 mice, Wilcoxon's signed-rank test) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements with statistical testing and reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency vs. running acceleration relationship was significantly lower during darkness.
source: In fact, the y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency vs. running acceleration relationship was significantly lower during darkness (t-statistic: 8.115, p=1.16×10−6, n = 15 mice, Student's paired t-test) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (t-test) and visual representation in Figure 1F.

claim: The decrease in theta rhythmic firing frequency during darkness is largely attributed to a decrease in the slope of its relationship to running speed.
source: We observed a decrease in theta rhythmic firing frequency during the dark condition (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 7). Similar to the observed changes in the LFP theta frequency, the decrease in theta rhythmic firing frequency was largely attributed to a decrease in the slope of its relationship to running speed (Figure 2C) as previously shown in rats (Hinman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by observed data in Figure 2B, 2C and supplementary figure 7, with citation to previous work in rats.

claim: The frequency of theta rhythmic firing increased with running speed during the light condition but not during the dark condition.
source: The frequency of theta rhythmic firing increased with running speed during the light condition (p=4.2×10–8, linear mixed effects model), but not during the dark condition (p=0.8085, linear mixed effects model; significant difference in slopes between light and dark, p=6.8×10–6) (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using linear mixed effects model and visual representation in Figure 2F.

claim: The magnitude of theta rhythmic firing increased with running speed during the light condition but not during the dark condition.
source: Similarly, the magnitude of theta rhythmic firing increased with running speed during the light condition (p=0.0002, linear mixed effects model), but not during the dark condition (p=0.0845, linear mixed effects model; difference in slopes between light and dark, p=9.1×10–6) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using linear mixed effects model and visual representation in Figure 2G.

claim: Phase locking of theta rhythmic neurons increased during the dark condition.
source: Interestingly, phase locking of theta rhythmic neurons increased during the dark condition (median MRL (Light) = 0.29, median MRL (Dark) = 0.37, p=1×10–32, Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of mean resultant length (MRL) with statistical testing and visual representation in Figure 3B.

claim: Each neuron's preferred phase of firing remained unchanged between light and dark conditions.
source: Notably, each neuron's preferred phase of firing remained unchanged between light and dark conditions (Figure 3C & D).
evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figures 3C and 3D showing correlation of preferred phases between conditions.

claim: 139 out of 842 neurons (16.5%) showed positive modulation of firing rates by visual inputs.
source: Positive modulation by visual inputs was observed ~4 times more frequently than negative modulation (139 out of 842 or 16.5% positively modulated neurons; 32 out of 842 or 3.8% negatively modulated neurons at significance level alpha = 0.05; data from 15 mice).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of neuronal responses across 842 neurons from 15 mice.

claim: 32 out of 842 neurons (3.8%) showed negative modulation of firing rates by visual inputs.
source: Positive modulation by visual inputs was observed ~4 times more frequently than negative modulation (139 out of 842 or 16.5% positively modulated neurons; 32 out of 842 or 3.8% negatively modulated neurons at significance level alpha = 0.05; data from 15 mice).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of neuronal responses across 842 neurons from 15 mice.

claim: The running speed-dependent gains in firing rate of MEC speed cells remain unaltered during the absence of visual inputs.
source: In summary, these data demonstrate that the running speed-dependent gains in firing rate of MEC speed cells remain unaltered during the absence of visual inputs, even if mean firing rates and the slopes of speed tuning curves change substantially.
evidence: Supported by analysis of speed response curves after normalization within conditions (Figure 5D and Table 6).

claim: No significant difference was observed between speed responses of positively speed-modulated neurons in the dark condition compared to the light condition after correcting for changes in mean firing rate.
source: In particular, no significant difference was observed between speed responses of positively speed-modulated neurons in the dark condition compared to the light condition (Table 6).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis presented in Table 6.

claim: Speed scores of all speed-modulated neurons were not significantly changed between light and dark conditions on the population level.
source: Likewise, speed scores (Pearson's correlation coefficient between firing rate and running speed) of all speed-modulated neurons were not significantly changed between light and dark conditions on the population level (p=0.912, n = 164, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) (Figure 5E) and were highly correlated between light and dark conditions on the single cell level (R = 0.86) (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) and correlation analysis, with visual representation in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: Spatial periodicity of grid cell firing was low in the initial dark session and strongly increased during the first light session.
source: We found that spatial periodicity of grid cell firing was low—but not completely eliminated—in the initial dark session and then strongly increased during the first light session (Figure 6A & B).
evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figures 6A and 6B showing firing rate maps and grid scores across sequential sessions.

claim: After initial orientation in light, spatial periodicity of grid cell firing decreased again after removal of visual inputs but remained significantly higher than in the initial dark session.
source: Interestingly, after this initial orientation, spatial periodicity of grid cell firing decreased again after removal of visual inputs, but remained significantly higher than in the initial dark session (Chi-square = 10.89, p=0.0043, n = 9 cells from two mice, Friedman test; post-hoc tests revealed p<0.05 comparing initial dark and light, and initial dark and second dark sessions).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Friedman test with post-hoc comparisons) of grid scores across sequential dark-light-dark sessions.

claim: Grid cell field centers remained stable, but grid fields appeared wider during complete darkness.
source: We found that grid cell field centers remained stable, but grid fields appeared wider during complete darkness (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by visual comparison of firing rate maps in Figure 6C.

claim: Grid scores and spatial information of grid cells showed significant decreases during darkness.
source: Quantification of spatial periodicity and spatial precision of grid cell firing by computing grid scores and spatial information (see Materials and methods) revealed a significant decrease in both spatial periodicity and spatial precision of spike locations (Figure 6D & E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis with visual representation in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: Spatiotemporal correlation between observed firing rate and expected firing rate from position showed significant reduction during complete darkness.
source: The results show a significant reduction in spatiotemporal correlation during complete darkness (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of spatiotemporal correlation with visual representation in Figure 6F.

claim: Grid scores computed from spike-triggered firing rate maps showed significant decrease in darkness.
source: Nevertheless, we observed a significant decrease in the grid scores computed from spike-triggered firing rate maps (p=0.0354, n = 15 cells, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2A) suggesting that the phase of each grid map remained stable in darkness.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) of grid scores from spike-triggered firing rate maps.

claim: Grid spacing remained unchanged in darkness (median grid spacing = 42 cm in light and dark).
source: Lastly, we measured the grid spacing in each of the spike-triggered firing rate maps. Grid spacing remained unchanged in darkness (median grid spacing = 42 cm in light and dark, p=1, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Bayes factor = 0.2005) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements with statistical testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and Bayesian analysis.

claim: Head direction cells maintained their head direction preference in the dark condition.
source: Interestingly, head direction cells maintained their head direction preference in the dark condition (Figure 7A & B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) suggesting that animals remained oriented within the environment during complete darkness.
evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figures 7A, 7B and supplementary figure 1 showing maintained preferred head directions.

claim: The mean resultant lengths of head directional firing rate maps were decreased in the dark condition.
source: However, the mean resultant lengths of head directional firing rate maps were decreased in the dark condition (Cohen's d = 0.238, p=0.0337, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) suggesting that the accuracy of head directional tuning was reduced in darkness (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test with effect size) and visual representation in Figure 7C.

claim: Border scores were significantly decreased during darkness.
source: Border scores were significantly decreased during darkness (Cohen's d = –0.4975, p=0.0325, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 7E) suggesting that representations of boundaries in the open-field environment were less accurate during darkness.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test with effect size) and visual representation in Figure 7E.

claim: Grid cell stability measured as spatiotemporal correlation was strongly correlated with the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship (R = 0.966, p=1.83×10–21).
source: Intriguingly, grid cell stability measured as spatiotemporal correlation of grid cell firing was strongly correlated with the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship (R = 0.966, p=1.83×10–21, n = 36 (18 time points x two conditions); Figure 8F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in Figure 8F and supplementary figure 1.

claim: The time courses of changes in grid cell stability and the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship were correlated within light and dark conditions.
source: The time courses of changes in grid cell stability and the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship were also correlated within light and dark conditions (Light: R = 0.825, p=2.55×10–5, n = 18 time points; Dark: R = 0.490, p=0.039, n = 18 time points) further confirming the link between grid cell stability and the LFP theta frequency to running speed relationship.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis within each condition separately.

claim: Changes in the y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship were negatively correlated with changes in grid cell stability in the light condition but uncorrelated in the dark condition.
source: In contrast, changes in the y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship as a function of time were negatively correlated with changes in grid cell stability in the light condition (R = –0.633, p=0.0048, n = 18 time points) and uncorrelated to changes in grid cell stability in the dark condition (R = 0.056, p=0.83, n = 18 time points) (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in supplementary figure 2.

claim: Grid cell firing is a function of velocity signals integrated over past time.
source: Finally, changes in spatial accuracy of grid cell firing on a 10 s time scale suggest that grid cell firing is a function of velocity signals integrated over past time.
evidence: Inferred from the observed slow saturating exponential changes in grid cell spatial accuracy over tens of seconds.

claim: Sensory inputs other than visual inputs can support grid cell firing, though less accurately, in complete darkness.
source: Moreover, we provide evidence that sensory inputs other than visual inputs can support grid cell firing, though less accurately, in complete darkness.
evidence: Supported by observations that grid cells maintain some spatial periodicity in darkness, though with reduced accuracy.

claim: Visual inputs do not alter the running speed-dependent gain in neuronal firing rates.
source: In contrast, visual inputs do not alter the running speed-dependent gain in neuronal firing rates.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing no significant changes in speed response curves after normalization within conditions (Figure 5D, Table 6).

claim: Changes in spatial stability of grid cell firing correlate with changes in a proposed speed signal by local field potential theta frequency.
source: By examining the temporal correlations between grid cell spatial stability and the two proposed speed signals—by firing rate or theta oscillations—we test if observed changes in grid cell firing can be explained by changes in the speed signal by firing rate or changes in the speed signal by LFP theta frequency.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis showing strong relationship between grid cell stability and LFP theta frequency slope (Figure 8F).

claim: The spatially periodic firing of grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex is widely recognized as a neuronal correlate of memory-guided and/or self-motion-based spatial navigation.
source: The spatially periodic firing of grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) (Fyhn et al., 2008; Fyhn et al., 2004; Hafting et al., 2005) is widely recognized as a neuronal correlate of memory-guided and/or self-motion-based spatial navigation (McNaughton et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on grid cells.

claim: Computational models of grid cells suggest that grid cells integrate running direction and traveled distance to maintain a spatially periodic firing pattern during path integration.
source: Based on that idea, computational models of grid cells including attractor network models (Burak and Fiete, 2009; Fuhs and Touretzky, 2006), oscillatory interference models (Blair et al., 2008; Burgess, 2008; Burgess et al., 2007; Hasselmo, 2008; Zilli and Hasselmo, 2010), hybrid models of attractor networks and oscillatory interference (Bush and Burgess, 2014), and probabilistic learning models (Cheung, 2016) suggest that grid cells integrate running direction and traveled distance to maintain a spatially periodic firing pattern during path integration (Gil et al., 2018; Jacob et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple computational modeling studies.

claim: Path integration depends on a velocity signal which depends on vestibular and proprioceptive signals and also moving sensory features such as optic flow.
source: Path integration depends on a velocity signal which depends on vestibular and proprioceptive signals (Chen et al., 2019; Tennant et al., 2018) and also moving sensory features such as optic flow (Campbell et al., 2018; Raudies et al., 2012; Raudies and Hasselmo, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on velocity signals in path integration.

claim: Any path integration mechanism ultimately suffers from the accumulation of error over distance traveled or elapsed time necessitating error correction by static environmental sensory inputs.
source: However, any path integration mechanism ultimately suffers from the accumulation of error over distance traveled or elapsed time (Kraus et al., 2015; Sreenivasan and Fiete, 2011) necessitating error correction by static environmental sensory inputs (Evans et al., 2016; Giocomo, 2016) such as visual landmark cues (Campbell et al., 2018; Hafting et al., 2005) or environmental boundaries (Barry et al., 2007; Hardcastle et al., 2015) to maintain an accurate representation of relative self-location within a spatial environment.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on error accumulation in path integration and error correction mechanisms.

claim: Self-motion-based signals such as head direction are necessary for grid cell firing.
source: Self-motion-based signals such as head direction are necessary for grid cell firing (Campbell et al., 2018; Winter et al., 2015b), and grid cell firing persists during darkness with reduced spatial selectivity (Allen et al., 2014; Hafting et al., 2005) reflecting the loss of error correction by visual cues.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies on grid cell firing requirements.

claim: Two recent studies on mice reported a rapid and nearly complete loss of spatially periodic grid cell firing during complete darkness.
source: In contrast, two more recent studies on mice reported a rapid and nearly complete loss of spatially periodic grid cell firing during complete darkness (Chen et al., 2016; Pérez-Escobar et al., 2016) suggesting that spatially periodic grid cell firing and path integration depend on error correction by visual cues.
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies on mice showing loss of grid cell firing in darkness.

claim: Motion-related interoceptive representations can combine with visual representations to form a single multimodal representation supporting path integration.
source: However, motion-related interoceptive representations, such as proprioceptive, vestibular, and motor efference copy signals, can combine with visual representations to form a single multimodal representation supporting path integration (Tcheang et al., 2011) suggesting that external sensory cues other than visual cues may be sufficient to stabilize grid cells and support path integration.
evidence: Supported by citation to study on multimodal sensory integration in path integration.

claim: Environmental novelty selectively reduces the slope of the LFP theta vs. running speed relationship and results in an increase in grid scale.
source: Interestingly, environmental novelty selectively reduces the slope of the LFP theta vs. running speed relationship (Jeewajee et al., 2008b; Wells et al., 2013) and also results in an increase in grid scale (Barry et al., 2012) as predicted by oscillatory interference models of grid cell firing (Burgess, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on effects of environmental novelty on theta dynamics and grid scale.

claim: The y-intercept of the LFP theta vs. running speed relationship has been linked to emotion-sensitivity, in particular anxiolysis.
source: In contrast, the y-intercept of the LFP theta vs. running speed relationship has been linked to emotion-sensitivity, in particular anxiolysis (Korotkova et al., 2018; Monaghan et al., 2017; Wells et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies linking theta frequency y-intercept to emotional states.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of MSDB neurons strongly reduces both theta oscillations and spatial periodicity of grid cell firing in the MEC.
source: In contrast to the speed signal by firing rate (Dannenberg et al., 2019; Hinman et al., 2016), the theta oscillatory speed signal depends on the MSDB (Chrobak et al., 1989; Dannenberg et al., 2015; Givens and Olton, 1994; Hinman et al., 2016; Lawson and Bland, 1993), and pharmacological inactivation of MSDB neurons strongly reduces both theta oscillations and spatial periodicity of grid cell firing in the MEC (Brandon et al., 2011; Koenig et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on effects of MSDB inactivation on theta and grid cells.

claim: Passive transportation of rats reduces theta oscillatory power and abolishes both spatially periodic grid cell firing and the speed signal by LFP theta frequency.
source: Furthermore, passive transportation of rats reduces theta oscillatory power and abolishes both spatially periodic grid cell firing and the speed signal by LFP theta frequency (Winter et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on effects of passive transportation on grid cells and theta.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the vestibular system or preventing linear/translational head movements abolish the modulation of LFP theta frequency by running speed and are associated with a decrease in the spatial information score and an increase in grid scale.
source: Likewise, pharmacological inactivation of the vestibular system or preventing linear/translational head movements in a virtual reality setup abolish the modulation of LFP theta frequency by running speed and are associated with a decrease in the spatial information score and an increase in grid scale (Chen et al., 2018; Jacob et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on vestibular system and head movement effects on theta and grid cells.

claim: The increase in grid scale observed during path integration on a circular track is associated with a change in the frequency of LFP theta oscillations, but not with a change in the firing patterns of speed and head direction cells.
source: Interestingly, the increase in grid scale observed during path integration on a circular track is associated with a change in the frequency of LFP theta oscillations, but not with a change in the firing patterns of speed and head direction cells (Jacob et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on grid scale changes during circular track navigation.

claim: Artificial low-theta stimulation can affect an animal's estimation of linear distance during approaches to a goal zone.
source: Moreover, a recent study demonstrated that artificial low-theta stimulation can affect an animal's estimation of linear distance during approaches to a goal zone (Mouchati et al., 2020) further strengthening a potential link between LFP theta frequency and path integration.
evidence: Supported by citation to study on effects of theta stimulation on distance estimation.

claim: Speed modulation of hippocampal theta frequency has been shown to correlate with spatial memory performance.
source: In addition, speed modulation of hippocampal theta frequency has been shown to correlate with spatial memory performance (Richard et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on theta frequency and spatial memory.

claim: Theta signals within the hippocampal formation have been suggested to reflect alterations in sensorimotor integration and the flow of sensory input, as well as distinct cognitive operations.
source: Theta signals within the hippocampal formation have been suggested to not only reflect alterations in sensorimotor integration and the flow of sensory input, but also distinct cognitive operations (Hinman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on theta signals and cognitive operations.

claim: Much of theta physiology and function seems to be shared across rodents and primates including the correlation of theta frequency with movement speed.
source: Furthermore, much of theta physiology and function seems to be shared across rodents and primates including the correlation of theta frequency with movement speed (Goyal et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to study on theta physiology across species.

claim: Increased phase locking has been associated with dynamical switching between encoding and retrieval dynamics.
source: Increased phase locking has been associated with dynamical switching between encoding and retrieval dynamics (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Siegle and Wilson, 2014), memory performance (Liebe et al., 2012; Rutishauser et al., 2010; Schomburg et al., 2014), and spatial cognitive demand (Barry et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on phase locking and cognitive functions.

claim: The number of theta rhythmic neurons increased sharply from 181 during immobility to 287 at the onset of running in the light condition.
source: In the light condition, the number of significantly theta rhythmic neurons increased sharply from 181 during immobility to 287 at the onset of running.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of theta rhythmic neurons as a function of running speed (Figure 2E).

claim: In the dark condition, the number of significantly theta rhythmic neurons sharply increased at the onset of running and then saturated close to the maximal number.
source: In contrast, the number of significantly theta rhythmic neurons sharply increased at the onset of running and then saturated close to the maximal number during darkness (157 during immobility, 322, 326, and 328 out of 339 neurons at higher running speeds) (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The ensemble of theta rhythmic neurons decreased with running speed in the light condition but increased to ceiling during the dark condition.
source: These data demonstrate that the ensemble of theta rhythmic neurons decreased with running speed in the light condition but increased to ceiling during the dark condition (Figure 2E) contributing to the stronger synchrony of theta rhythmic firing observed on the population level (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Both the frequency and magnitude of theta rhythmic firing was higher in putative principal neurons compared to putative interneurons.
source: In general, both the frequency and magnitude of theta rhythmic firing was higher in PNs compared to INs (Figure 2—figure supplements 2C and 3C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of theta rhythmic firing properties between cell types shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Changes in theta rhythmic spiking activity as a function of running speed during and between light and dark conditions were similar across grid cells, head direction cells, and border cells.
source: We found that changes in theta rhythmic spiking activity as a function of running speed during and between light and dark conditions were similar across grid cells, head direction cells, and border cells (Figure 2—figure supplements 4, 5 and 6) and indistinguishable from all PNs, indicating that changes in theta rhythmic activity is ubiquitous across different functional cell types in the medial entorhinal cortex.
evidence: Supported by analysis across different functional cell types shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Changes in firing rates and theta rhythmic firing are primarily driven by changes in net excitatory input from visual cortex and do not reflect changes in the perception of the spatial aspects of the environment.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that changes in firing rates and theta rhythmic firing are primarily driven by changes in net excitatory input from visual cortex and do not reflect changes in the perception of the spatial aspects of the environment.
evidence: Inferred from observations that spatially non-informative light stimulation produces similar effects as light-dark transitions (Figure 4E & F).

claim: Changes in retinal stimulation due to changes in the amount of spatially non-informative light hitting the retina are sufficient to explain the observed changes in mean firing rates of MEC neurons.
source: In summary, these data demonstrate that the changes in retinal stimulation due to changes in the amount of spatially non-informative light hitting the retina after transitioning from dark to light and vice versa are sufficient to explain the observed changes in mean firing rates of MEC neurons.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic control experiments showing similar effects with spatially non-informative light (Figure 4E & F).

claim: Animals need an initial orientation in the environment supported by static visual cues but can then use sensory cues other than visual cues to roughly maintain that orientation over long time periods.
source: Taken together, the data presented in this study suggest that animals need an initial orientation in the environment supported by static visual cues but can then use sensory cues other than visual cues, including wall encounters, to roughly maintain that orientation over long time periods.
evidence: Inferred from observations that grid cells maintain orientation, phase, and scale in darkness after initial light exposure (Figure 6A & B).

claim: For maintaining a spatial representation in a completely dark environment, vestibular signals, motor efference copies, proprioceptive feedback, and external geometrical cues may be sufficient to maintain the orientation, scale, and phase of grid cell firing fields.
source: For maintaining a spatial representation in a completely dark environment, vestibular signals, motor efference copies, proprioceptive feedback, and external geometrical cues may be sufficient to maintain the orientation, scale, and phase of grid cell firing fields.
evidence: Inferred from observations that grid cells maintain basic spatial properties in darkness.

claim: During the light condition, static visual cues may offer additional cues to self-location since the distance and direction to these cues systematically change with the animal's movement, and optic flow may be used for refining an estimate of self-motion.
source: During the light condition, static visual cues may offer additional cues to self-location since the distance and direction to these cues systematically change with the animal's movement, and optic flow may be used for refining an estimate of self-motion.
evidence: Speculative explanation for improved spatial accuracy in light condition.

claim: The representation of space in a cognitive map may integrate velocity signals over past time and may therefore be history-dependent and updated at a slow behavioral time scale.
source: Slow changes in both the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship and the spatial periodicity of grid cells after transitions between light and dark conditions suggest that the representation of space in a cognitive map may integrate velocity signals over past time and may therefore be history-dependent and updated at a slow behavioral time scale.
evidence: Inferred from observed slow saturating exponential changes in grid cell stability and theta frequency slope (Figure 8).

claim: The result of integrating velocity signals over time would be a representation of space which is malleable by internal memory processes.
source: The result of such an integration would be a representation of space which is malleable by internal memory processes.
evidence: Speculative conclusion based on observed temporal dynamics of spatial representations.

claim: The observed decrease in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship is independent from the decrease in running acceleration during darkness.
source: We therefore examined if the observed decrease in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship is independent from the decrease in running acceleration during darkness. If truly independent, the y-intercept of the correlation between LFP theta frequency and running acceleration is expected to decrease during the dark condition. In fact, the y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency vs. running acceleration relationship was significantly lower during darkness (t-statistic: 8.115, p=1.16×10−6, n = 15 mice, Student's paired t-test) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of theta frequency vs acceleration relationship showing decreased y-intercept in darkness.

claim: Restricting analysis of the LFP theta frequency to running speed analysis to time points when running acceleration was near zero did not significantly change speed tuning curves of LFP theta frequency.
source: Furthermore, restricting our analysis of the LFP theta frequency to running speed analysis to time points when running acceleration was near zero (0 ± 5 cm/s2) did not significantly change speed tuning curves of LFP theta frequency (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by analysis controlling for acceleration effects shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The LFP theta frequency is directly modulated by running speed.
source: These data demonstrate that the LFP theta frequency is directly modulated by running speed and that the observed change in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship in darkness reflects a change in visual inputs.
evidence: Supported by analysis controlling for acceleration effects (Figure 1F & G).

claim: The observed change in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship in darkness reflects a change in visual inputs.
source: These data demonstrate that the LFP theta frequency is directly modulated by running speed and that the observed change in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship in darkness reflects a change in visual inputs.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing changes persist after controlling for acceleration and other confounds.

claim: The LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationships in light and dark became more different with elapsed time after start of light and dark epochs at a time scale of tens of seconds.
source: Averaging data from 78 sessions from 14 mice, we found that the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationships in light and dark became more different with elapsed time after start of light and dark epochs at a time scale of tens of seconds (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 1H and supplementary figure 1B.

claim: The divergence in theta frequency vs running speed relationships between light and dark appeared to be largely driven by a change in the slope as opposed to changes in the y-intercept.
source: This divergence appeared to be largely driven by a change in the slope of the theta frequency vs. running speed relationship as opposed to changes in the y-intercept.
evidence: Inferred from visual inspection and quantitative analysis of slope and y-intercept changes over time.

claim: There was a slow increase in slope over time during the light condition (Pearson's R = 0.79, p=0.0001) and a slow decrease in slope over time during the dark condition (Pearson's R = −0.79, p=0.0001).
source: This analysis revealed a slow increase in slope over time during the light condition (Pearson's R = 0.79, p=0.0001) and a slow decrease in slope over time during the dark condition (Pearson's R = −0.79, p=0.0001) (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in Figure 1I.

claim: The increase in slope during the light condition was accompanied by a small, yet significant, decrease in the y-intercept (Pearson's R = −0.77, p=0.0002).
source: The increase in slope during the light condition was accompanied by a small, yet significant, decrease in the y-intercept (Pearson's R = −0.77, p=0.0002) (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in Figure 1J.

claim: The y-intercept did not change significantly over time during the dark condition (Pearson's R = −0.16, p=0.5251).
source: In contrast, the y-intercept did not change significantly over time during the dark condition (Pearson's R = −0.16, p=0.5251) (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with visual representation in Figure 1J.

claim: There were fast (<10 s) light-to-dark decreases and dark-to-light increases in the slope and y-intercept of the LFP theta frequency to running speed relationship.
source: In addition to those slow components of change, analyzing the transition points between light and dark conditions revealed fast (<10 s) light-to-dark decreases and dark-to-light increases in the slope (Figure 1K) and y-intercept (Figure 1L) of the LFP theta frequency to running speed relationship.
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis around transition points shown in Figures 1K and 1L.

claim: Many neurons in the MEC show a theta rhythmic firing pattern and the frequency of theta rhythmic firing increases with running speed.
source: Local field potential activity in the MEC primarily reflects the summed activity of synaptic inputs to the MEC, which is likely to be correlated with firing patterns of MEC neurons. Many neurons in the MEC show a theta rhythmic firing pattern and—similarly to the LFP theta frequency—the frequency of theta rhythmic firing increases with running speed (Hinman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and general knowledge about MEC neuronal properties.

claim: 339 out of 342 theta modulated neurons could be analyzed using the MLE model of theta rhythmic firing.
source: For each neuron, an autocorrelogram model was fitted to each of those 10 s blocks of data using the MLE approach. For each of those 10 s blocks of data, the average theta rhythmic firing frequency across neurons could then be computed from the peaks of the average autocorrelogram model across neurons by taking the inverse of the first peak in the autocorrelogram model. To analyze running speed-dependent theta rhythmic firing on the population level, we first identified continuous epochs of running speed within the ranges of 0–3 cm/s (immobility), 5–10 cm/s, 10–15 cm/s, 15–20 cm/s, and 20–25 cm/s. We next used the MLE approach to model an autocorrelogram for each running speed bin of each neuron. Neurons with sufficient number of spikes resulting in at least 100 interspike intervals to compute an MLE-modeled autocorrelogram in at least one of the running speed bins were included into the analysis (n = 339 neurons).
evidence: Stated as part of the methods and results for theta rhythmic firing analysis.

claim: The frequency of theta rhythmic firing was significantly reduced in the dark condition (effect size: –0.381 Hz, t-statistic: –8.598, df: 4316, p=1×10–17).
source: The frequency of theta rhythmic firing was significantly reduced in the dark condition (effect size: –0.381 Hz, t-statistic: –8.598, df: 4316, p=1×10–17, CI: [–0.468 –0.294]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of theta rhythmic firing frequency across conditions.

claim: There was a fast decrease in the frequency of theta rhythmic firing when transitioning from light to dark and a fast increase when transitioning from dark to light.
source: Similar to the fast initial changes observed in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship, we observed a fast decrease in the frequency of theta rhythmic firing when transitioning from light to dark and a fast increase when transitioning from dark to light (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis around transition points shown in Figure 2I.

claim: In contrast to the observed changes in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship, the frequency of theta rhythmic firing did not further change on a time scale of tens of seconds during light or dark epochs.
source: In contrast to the observed changes in the slope of the LFP theta frequency vs. running speed relationship, the frequency of theta rhythmic firing did not further change on a time scale of tens of seconds during light or dark epochs.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of temporal dynamics between LFP theta frequency slope and single neuron theta rhythmic firing frequency.

claim: Differentiating between putative principal neurons and interneurons revealed a decrease in frequency of theta rhythmic firing as a function of time in both light and dark conditions in interneurons but not principal neurons.
source: However, differentiating between PNs and INs revealed a decrease in frequency of theta rhythmic firing as a function of time in both light and dark conditions in INs but not PNs (Figure 2—figure supplements 2F and 3E).
evidence: Supported by cell-type specific analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The time course of changes in theta-frequency phase locking was similar to the changes in the frequency of theta rhythmic spiking, showing a fast initial change but no further slow component of change.
source: We next investigated the time course of those changes in phase locking (Figure 3E). The time course of changes in theta-frequency phase locking was similar to the changes in the frequency of theta rhythmic spiking, showing a fast initial change but no further slow component of change.
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No differences in theta-frequency phase locking were observed between putative principal neurons and interneurons.
source: No significant differences were observed between PNs and INs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Notably, each neuron's preferred phase of firing remained unchanged between light and dark conditions (Figure 3C & D). We next investigated the time course of those changes in phase locking (Figure 3E). The time course of changes in theta-frequency phase locking was similar to the changes in the frequency of theta rhythmic spiking, showing a fast initial change but no further slow component of change. No differences were observed between PNs and INs.
evidence: Stated explicitly with reference to supplementary figure 1.

claim: The observed changes in the slope of speed tuning curves are caused by changes in mean firing rate rather than changes in the running speed-dependent gain in firing rates.
source: To address the question whether the observed changes in the slope of speed response curves are caused by changes in the running speed-dependent gain in firing rates or are instead artifacts of changes in the mean firing rate of neurons, we compared speed response curves between light and dark conditions after normalization within conditions as opposed to normalization across conditions. Note that normalization within conditions corrects for changes in mean firing rate between conditions. Interestingly, we found that speed response curves appeared very similar between light and dark conditions after correcting for changes in mean firing rate and conjunctive coding properties (Figure 5B &D).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of speed response curves with different normalization methods (Figure 5).

claim: The numbers of speed-modulated cells with conjunctive coding of position, head direction and theta phase were unchanged in the dark condition.
source: Moreover, the numbers of speed-modulated cells with conjunctive coding of position, head direction and theta phase were unchanged in the dark condition (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Grid fields appear wider in darkness because the spatiotemporal accuracy of grid cell firing is reduced without changes in the phase, orientation, or spacing of grid maps.
source: Taken together, these data support the hypothesis that grid fields in the firing rate map appear broader because the spatiotemporal accuracy of grid cell firing is reduced without changes in the phase, orientation, or spacing of grid maps.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of spike-triggered firing rate maps showing maintained spacing, phase, and orientation but reduced grid scores (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).

claim: Animals remained oriented within the environment during complete darkness.
source: Interestingly, head direction cells maintained their head direction preference in the dark condition (Figure 7A & B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) suggesting that animals remained oriented within the environment during complete darkness.
evidence: Inferred from observation that head direction cells maintained their preferred directions in darkness.

claim: The accuracy of head directional tuning was reduced in darkness.
source: However, the mean resultant lengths of head directional firing rate maps were decreased in the dark condition (Cohen's d = 0.238, p=0.0337, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) suggesting that the accuracy of head directional tuning was reduced in darkness (Figure 7C).
evidence: Inferred from decreased mean resultant lengths of head direction tuning curves.

claim: Representations of boundaries in the open-field environment were less accurate during darkness.
source: Border scores were significantly decreased during darkness (Cohen's d = –0.4975, p=0.0325, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 7E) suggesting that representations of boundaries in the open-field environment were less accurate during darkness.
evidence: Inferred from decreased border scores in darkness.

claim: Grid cell firing may be more strongly associated with changes in the mean attractor state of rhythmic firing in the MEC reflected by changes in the LFP theta signal than with changes in the rhythmic firing of individual neurons.
source: These data on the parallel time course of changes in the oscillatory speed signal by LFP theta frequency and grid cell stability suggest that grid cell firing may be more strongly associated with changes in the mean attractor state of rhythmic firing in the MEC reflected by changes in the LFP theta signal than with changes in the rhythmic firing of individual neurons.
evidence: Inferred from observation that LFP theta frequency slope changes match grid cell stability changes over time, while single neuron theta rhythmic firing shows only fast changes.

claim: The exponential change in LFP theta may reflect a slow change in an oscillatory speed signal arising from other cortical structures such as the medial septum.
source: Alternately, the exponential change in LFP theta may reflect a slow change in an oscillatory speed signal arising from other cortical structures such as the medial septum.
evidence: Speculative alternative explanation for observed temporal dynamics.

claim: In a novel environment, a reduced slope in the LFP theta frequency to running speed relationship may be the consequence of underestimating the distances between borders resulting in a larger grid scale.
source: Taken together, these data may indicate that in a novel environment, a reduced slope in the LFP theta frequency to running speed relationship may be the consequence of underestimating the distances between borders resulting in a larger grid scale but that in a familiar environment, the lack of error correction in a path integration mechanism may result in a reduction of the dynamic range in an oscillatory speed signal by LFP theta frequency resulting in less accurate speed coding.
evidence: Speculative interpretation integrating current findings with previous literature on novelty effects.

claim: In a familiar environment, the lack of error correction in a path integration mechanism may result in a reduction of the dynamic range in an oscillatory speed signal by LFP theta frequency resulting in less accurate speed coding.
source: Taken together, these data may indicate that in a novel environment, a reduced slope in the LFP theta frequency to running speed relationship may be the consequence of underestimating the distances between borders resulting in a larger grid scale but that in a familiar environment, the lack of error correction in a path integration mechanism may result in a reduction of the dynamic range in an oscillatory speed signal by LFP theta frequency resulting in less accurate speed coding.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of current findings in familiar environment context.

claim: The reduction in spatial accuracy of grid cell firing during darkness is accompanied by a reduction of accuracy in head directional tuning and a reduction of spatial accuracy of border cell firing.
source: Data presented in this study also show that the reduction in spatial accuracy of grid cell firing is accompanied by a reduction of accuracy in head directional tuning and a reduction of spatial accuracy of border cell firing (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by data showing concurrent reductions in grid cell, head direction cell, and border cell accuracy (Figure 7).

claim: An alternative explanation for the observed reduction of spatial accuracy in grid cell firing during darkness is a reduction of accuracy in head directional signals, boundary signals, or both due to the loss of visual information.
source: An alternative explanation for the observed reduction of spatial accuracy in grid cell firing during darkness is therefore a reduction of accuracy in head directional signals (Winter et al., 2015a), boundary signals, or both due to the loss of visual information.
evidence: Proposed as alternative explanation with citation to relevant work.

claim: The frequency of theta rhythmic firing of MEC neurons may serve as a speed signal that is integrated over longer time scales than previously accounted for by computational models of grid cells.
source: Another possibility is that the frequency of theta rhythmic firing of MEC neurons serves as a speed signal that is integrated over longer time scales than previously accounted for by computational models of grid cells (Dannenberg et al., 2019).
evidence: Proposed as alternative explanation with citation to relevant work.

claim: Both the slope of the LFP theta frequency and spatial periodicity of grid cell firing would depend on the history of a velocity signal if theta rhythmic firing serves as a speed signal integrated over time.
source: In that scenario, both the slope of the LFP theta frequency and spatial periodicity of grid cell firing would depend on the history of a velocity signal, which would be consistent with the observed slow saturating exponential component of change.
evidence: Logical inference from the hypothesis that speed signals are integrated over time.

claim: Integration of velocity signals over seconds has previously been shown to optimize the proposed speed code by firing rate.
source: Such an integration over seconds has previously been shown to optimize the proposed speed code by firing rate (Dannenberg et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The slow component of change in spatial accuracy of grid cell firing cannot be explained by error accumulation alone.
source: Notably, the slow component of change in spatial accuracy of grid cell firing cannot be explained by error accumulation alone. While error accumulation could account for the observed slow decrease in spatial stability after removal of visual inputs, error accumulation cannot be the reason for the observed slow increase in spatial accuracy after reinstating visual inputs.
evidence: Logical argument based on asymmetry in temporal dynamics between light-to-dark and dark-to-light transitions.

claim: If signals required for grid cell firing are integrated over time, a slow increase in spatial accuracy after reinstating visual inputs is expected.
source: If signals required for grid cell firing are integrated over time, however, such a slow increase is expected.
evidence: Logical inference from the hypothesis of temporal integration of velocity signals.

claim: A similar increase in spatial accuracy of grid cell firing was reported by Weber and Sprekeler, 2019.
source: Notably, a similar increase in spatial accuracy of grid cell firing was also reported recently by Weber and Sprekeler, 2019.
evidence: Supported by citation to recent work showing similar findings.

claim: Future experimental and computational modeling studies are needed to address whether and how longer integration time windows could support grid cell firing.
source: Future experimental and computational modeling studies are needed to address the questions whether and how longer integration time windows could support grid cell firing.
evidence: Stated as a need for future research.

claim: Data were collected from a total of 17 adult 3–6 month-old male mice.
source: Data were collected from a total of 17 adult 3–6 month-old male mice (Mus musculus) of wild type and transgenic backgrounds (Wild type, C57Bl/6J; ChAT-IRES-Cre, B6;129S6-Chattm2(cre)Lowl/J; PV-IRES-Cre, B6;129P2-Pvalbtm1(cre)Arbr/J).
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods section describing subjects.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee for the Charles River Campus at Boston University.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee for the Charles River Campus at Boston University.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods section.

claim: Mice underwent surgery for implantation of 2 movable tetrodes targeting the superficial layers of the MEC in the left hemisphere.
source: Mice underwent surgery for implantation of 2 movable tetrodes targeting the superficial layers of the MEC in the left hemisphere.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods section describing subjects.

claim: The dark condition was completely dark from the perspective of the human experimenter after adaptation to the dark condition for at least five minutes.
source: The dark condition was completely dark from the perspective of the human experimenter after adaptation to the dark condition for at least five minutes.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods section describing behavior during light and dark conditions.

claim: Recordings only began when it was completely dark from the perspective of the human eye after having adopted to the dark condition for at least 5 min.
source: Importantly, the experimenter frequently tested for any potential light sources within or light leaks into the space around the open-field environment. Recordings only began when it was completely dark from the perspective of the human eye after having adopted to the dark condition for at least 5 min.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods section describing experimental procedures.

claim: A typical recording session lasted 40–60 min.
source: A typical recording session lasted 40–60 min.
evidence: Stated in Materials and methods section describing behavior during light and dark conditions.

claim: 28 cells from six mice were identified as grid cells based on their grid scores.
source: 28 cells from six mice were identified as grid cells based on their grid scores (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated in Results section on grid cell spatial firing.

claim: 67 cells with significant unidirectional head direction tuning were classified as head direction cells.
source: We identified 67 cells with significant unidirectional head direction tuning which were classified as head direction cells (Sargolini et al., 2006; Taube et al., 1990b; Taube et al., 1990a).
evidence: Stated in Results section on head direction cells with citations to classification methods.

claim: 27 border cells were identified.
source: In addition to grid cells, border or boundary vector cells (Lever et al., 2010; Solstad et al., 2008) are hypothesized to contribute to a representation of space in the MEC. We identified 27 border cells (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and compared their border scores (Solstad et al., 2008) between light and dark conditions.
evidence: Stated in Results section on border cells with citations to relevant work.
